system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2140-12-21 06:46:00 to 2140-12-22 18:30:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of pseudotumor cerebri and a VP shunt, previously repositioned for right lower quadrant pain, was readmitted due to recurrent sharp RLQ pain and nausea. Initial evaluation showed no evidence of infection, obstruction, or shunt displacement. Surgical consultation found no indication for intervention. Pain was managed with transition from short-acting opioids to scheduled OxyContin, resulting in improved control. Chronic conditions including diabetes, hypertension, depression, migraines, and obstructive sleep apnea were monitored. The patient was discharged home with a pain management plan, follow-up arranged with primary care and pain specialists, and recommendations to restart and re-evaluate CPAP therapy due to narcotic use.
problems: Migraine, unspecified, without mention of intractable migraine without mention of status migrainosus
Diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  ___ with history of pseudomotor cerebri, status post
shunt, assess for obstruction.

TECHNIQUE:  Three views of the abdomen and lower chest were obtained.

COMPARISON:  Prior abdominal radiograph from ___.

FINDINGS:VP shunt ends in the right mid abdomen. The bowel gas pattern is
normal.  There is no evidence of shunt kinking in the lower chest or abdomen;
position is unchanged from ___.  No free air.

IMPRESSION:  Normal shunt position.  No evidence of bowel obstruction or free
air.

INDICATION:  Right lower quadrant abdominal pain possibly related to VP shunt
placement.

COMPARISONS:  CT of the abdomen and pelvis from ___.

TECHNIQUE:  MDCT-acquired axial images of the abdomen and pelvis were obtained
without contrast.  Coronal and sagittal reformats reviewed.

DLP:  ___ mGy-cm.

FINDINGS:  The lower chest is remarkable only for linear atelectasis or
scarring in the left lower lobe.

The VP shunt catheter enters the anterior abdomen near the inferior edge of
the liver, course along the internal aspect of the right abdominal wall and
terminates just inferior to the liver edge (2:38).  There is no fluid
collection or mass at this location to indicate possible obstruction.

There are no focal liver lesions.  The patient is status post cholecystectomy.
The pancreas, adrenal glands, and spleen appear normal.  The right kidney
contains a 3.7 x 3.7 cm simple cyst (2:26).  There is a punctate,
non-obstructing stone in the left kidney (2:33).  There is no hydronephrosis. 
There are no stones along the course of either ureter.

The visualized loops of small and large bowel are unremarkable.  There is no
free fluid or air within the abdomen.  The appendix is not well visualized,
but there is no inflammatory change to suggest presence of acute appendicitis.

The patient is status post hysterectomy.  The urinary bladder appears normal. 
There is an unchanged ovoid calcified cyst in the pelvis.  There is no free
fluid, lymphadenopathy, or pelvic mass.

There are no focal osseous lesions concerning for malignancy.

IMPRESSION:  Unchanged appearance of ventriculoperitoneal shunt terminating in
the right lower quadrant of the abdomen without evidence of fluid collection
or mass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. You were admitted last night for right lower quadrant pain. Can you tell me more about the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s sharp and constant. It’s been worse over the past few days. I’ve had this since my shunt was placed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You have a VP shunt for pseudotumor cerebri. Did you have it adjusted recently?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, a few months ago because of the pain. But it didn’t help much. I heard on my last X-ray the shunt flipped—could that be causing this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I reviewed your KUB from yesterday. The radiologist says the shunt position is unchanged. There’s no sign it flipped or is kinked.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But the pain is real. I can barely walk when it flares up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I believe you. We’re not dismissing your pain. We just need to make sure there’s no emergency like infection or bowel issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. What tests did you do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked blood work—CBC, electrolytes, kidney and liver tests. All came back normal. Urine test was fine, and no signs of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the shunt? Could it be irritating something inside?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s possible. General surgery and neurosurgery both saw you. They don’t think surgery is needed now, but they recommend follow-up with neurosurgery to discuss possible shunt removal if pain continues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Removal? That sounds extreme. Is that safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s an option to consider later. Right now, we’re focusing on managing your pain and making sure no other issues are missed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. The pain meds in the ER didn’t help much. I had Dilaudid and lorazepam.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I saw that. We’re going to adjust your pain plan. We’re increasing your amitriptyline from 10mg to 25mg at night. It helps with nerve-type pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on that for migraines. Will it help this kind of pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can, especially when pain is chronic. We’re also starting a short course of Vicodin for breakthrough pain, just until you see your doctors after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds better. What about my diabetes? I usually take glyburide.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We held your oral diabetes meds temporarily and put you on insulin shots to keep your sugar stable while you're in pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. Will I go back to pills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll restart glyburide before you go home. Your blood sugar has been in good range.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my other meds—amlodipine, omeprazole, citalopram—I’ve been taking those for years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve continued all your regular medications: blood pressure, cholesterol, acid reflux, and depression meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been feeling more down lately. The pain makes everything harder.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. Chronic pain affects mood. We’re keeping your citalopram and increasing amitriptyline, which can also help with depression.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ve also been tired. Could that be low iron? My last doctor mentioned it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your primary care noted low iron. We’re starting ferrous sulfate 325mg daily to help with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And vitamin D? I think I’m low on that too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Your levels were low. We’re adding 400 units of vitamin D daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. One more thing—my liver tests were high before. Are they okay now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your alkaline phosphatase is still elevated, over 200, but other liver tests are normal. We don’t think it’s liver disease. Could be from meds or bone. We’ll follow up after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, as long as it’s not serious. I don’t want another hospital stay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. I wanted to update you. We did a CT scan this morning to double-check the shunt and abdomen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And? Did you see anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The shunt looks unchanged. It ends in the right lower abdomen, no fluid collection or mass. Bowel looks normal, no obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So nothing’s wrong with it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No surgical cause for the pain. Surgery and neurosurgery agree: no intervention needed now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll discharge you tomorrow morning. You’ll go home with the new pain plan: higher amitriptyline and Vicodin as needed. Follow up with your neurologist and primary care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the iron and vitamin D?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep taking both. Your PCP will check levels in a few weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the high alkaline phosphatase?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also something to follow up on as an outpatient. Likely not urgent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I feel better knowing there’s no emergency.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll get your discharge papers ready. You should be able to go home by tomorrow afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, just before discharge. How’s the pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. The new meds are helping. Still there, but more manageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good progress. Remember, take the amitriptyline at night, and Vicodin only if needed. Don’t drive on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And I’ll call my doctors to set up follow-ups.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take care, and I hope the pain continues to improve.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of pseudotumor cerebri and a VP shunt presented with persistent right lower quadrant abdominal pain. Evaluation included normal labs, a KUB showing unchanged shunt position, and a CT abdomen confirming no fluid collection, mass, or obstruction. Surgical and neurosurgical teams found no indication for intervention. Pain was managed with an increased dose of amitriptyline and a short course of hydrocodone. Her diabetes was managed with temporary insulin, later transitioning back to oral glyburide. Iron and vitamin D deficiencies were addressed with supplementation. She was discharged home with follow-up plans for pain management, depression, and monitoring of elevated alkaline phosphatase.
